links.note: 691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings (இகல்வேந்தர்) to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor closing in (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). In 1104 a lover asks where she got a fire that burns when he withdraws and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). The king's fire burns at close range and the lover's reverses that rule, so the court calls for a kept middle distance and the love speech for none.

691 compares the king to a fire one warms at from a measured distance. 896 says one burned by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார் பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகுவார்). Read together, the fire in 691 understates the danger: 896 ranks the offended great above fire, though Parimelazhagar takes its பெரியார் as those great in austerity, not kings.

692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those same kings; Parimelazhagar takes விழைப as the enjoyments, adornment and precedence proper to a king. 179 says Fortune herself comes to the wise who, knowing virtue, do not covet (அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும் ... திரு). Both make not-wanting the route by which wealth arrives, once as court prudence and once as virtue.

693 warns the servant that once suspicion has arisen it is hard for anyone to clear it (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது), so grave faults must be guarded against beforehand. 510 addresses the ruler: doubting one who has been examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்) brings trouble that does not end. The pair shows the same suspicion from both sides: the book counts it a fault in the king, yet tells the minister to plan as if it cannot be undone.

693 says those who would guard themselves should guard against the gravest things (போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as faults a king cannot forgive. 891 says not slighting the power of those able to act is the chief of all the guarding done by those who guard themselves (போற்றுவார் போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). Both use போற்றல் for self-protection and locate its first object in one's dealings with the powerful.

694 says that in the presence of the great one should suppress whispering and shared smiles (செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல்). 715 calls the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு) the best of good things. Court and assembly get the same rule of holding speech back before superiors; 694 extends it to private asides and laughter, which Parimelazhagar says the king would take as aimed at himself.

695 forbids the courtier to listen in on anything or press for it, and lets him hear a secret only when it is released (எப்பொருளும் ஓரார் தொடரார் ... விட்டக்கால் கேட்க மறை). 587 defines the spy as one able to hear what has been concealed (மறைந்தவை கேட்கவற்றாகி). Hearing hidden things is therefore not wrong in itself in this book: it is the spy's work directed outward, and what 695 bars is turning it on one's own king.

695 treats the king's secret (மறை) as something to be heard only when he lets it go. 1076 says the base are like a beaten drum because they carry to others the secrets they have heard (தாம் கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). The two give the two ends of handling a secret: restraint in acquiring it in 695, and the failure to hold it in 1076.

696 tells the minister to know the king's mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) before speaking. 687 ranks highest the envoy who knows what is due, considers the time and knows the place (கடனறிந்து காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து). The phrase காலங் கருதி is common to both, so the same discipline of timed speech is asked of the man at his own king's side and of the man sent to a foreign court.

696 limits what the minister says to things not disliked (வெறுப்பில) and said so that they are wanted (வேட்பச் சொலல்). 638 says that even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to tell him what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). They conflict if வெறுப்பில is read, with Parimelazhagar, as matters the king will not reject; if it means only an inoffensive manner, 696 governs how to say what 638 obliges one to say.

696 opens with குறிப்பறிந்து, knowing the king's mood, as the first condition of speaking to him. 701 praises the one who looks and knows what is meant without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்) as an ornament to the earth. The skill 696 names in passing is taken up as the subject of the next chapter, beginning with 701.

697 says to speak what is wanted and never to say what has no use, even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்). 200 gives the general rule: say words that have use, do not say words that have none (சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்). The court verse applies the household rule and tightens it, since here even the king's own request does not license useless talk.

698 says not to belittle the king as younger or as a relative, but to act in keeping with the light that rests on him (நின்ற ஒளியோடு ஒழுகப்படும்). 388 says a king who does justice and protects is set apart for the people as இறை (மக்கட்கு இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). Parimelazhagar reads the ஒளி of 698 as the king's godlike quality, so 388 supplies its ground: the standing comes from the office of protecting, which is why age and kinship do not touch it.

698 forbids belittling a king on the grounds of youth or kinship (இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார்). 667 says one must not scorn by outward form, since the great rolling chariot depends on its linchpin (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்). Both reject judging a person by a surface measure, whether age, family relation or size, and point instead to the function he carries.

699 says those of unshaken vision (துளக்கற்ற காட்சியவர்) will not do what is unacceptable on the thought that they are in favour. 654 says those of untrembling vision (நடுக்கற்ற காட்சியவர்) will not do what is degrading even when caught in trouble (இடுக்கண் படினும் இளிவந்த செய்யார்). The same formula is used for opposite pressures, so that steadiness is tested by favour in 699 as it is by hardship in 654.

700 says the familiarity (கெழுதகைமை) that does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதி) brings ruin. 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that in no way cuts down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு). The liberty that defines friendship between equals is thus withdrawn where the other party is a king, as Parimelazhagar reads 700.

700 says intimacy that does what is improper brings ruin (பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்). 805 says that when friends do something hurtful one should understand it as folly or as great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்). The conflict holds on Manakkudavar's gloss of 700, which speaks of the nature of friendship in general; on Parimelazhagar's, 700 concerns a king and the two verses address different relationships.

701 praises the one who knows what is meant by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 1100, in the love chapter that has the same title குறிப்பறிதல், says that when eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words have no use (வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல). Reading without speech is a minister's rare skill in 701 and the ordinary condition of two lovers in 1100.

702 says one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை) should be held equal to a god. 587 defines a spy as one able to hear what is concealed and to be without doubt about what he has learned (அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே ஒற்று). Both set the same standard, hidden things known with certainty; the spy reaches it through informants and the sign-reader by perception alone.

702 says the one who knows another's mind without doubt is to be taken as equal to a god (தெய்வத்தோ டொப்பக் கொளல்). 388 says the king who does justice and protects is set down as இறை for the people (இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). In both a human being is ranked with the divine for a capacity he exercises, and Parimelazhagar notes in each case that he is still a man by birth.

703 says to give whatever it takes from one's resources and secure those who read a sign by a sign (யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 794 says the friendship of one of good family who is ashamed of blame should be had even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு). The shared formula marks the two kinds of person the book thinks worth paying for, the perceptive adviser and the friend with a sense of shame.

703 urges the king to pay any price for those who read signs. 445 says that since counsellors serve as the ruler's eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக ஒழுகலான்), he must choose them with care. 445 gives the reason behind 703: the king sees through his advisers, so an adviser who can read what is unsaid is worth what Parimelazhagar lists as wealth, land, elephants and horses.

704 says those who grasp what is meant without being told and the rest are alike in limbs (உறுப்போ ரனையரால்) and yet different. 993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people (உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால்), and true likeness is likeness of character. Both deny that the shared body makes people alike, with perception the dividing line in 704 and பண்பு in 993.

704 says readers of the unspoken and others share the same limbs but are different (வேறு). 1071 says the base look just like people (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்), a resemblance the speaker has seen nowhere else. The same figure of outward human likeness hiding an inner difference serves a point about intelligence in 704 and about moral baseness in 1071.

704 stops at saying that those who cannot grasp the unspoken are 'different' (வேறு) from those who can. 410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). Parimelazhagar glosses the வேறு of 704 with this very comparison, the idea being that they are animals, so 410 states outright what 704 leaves implied.

705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read a sign by a sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). 574 asks what eyes without measured kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் ... கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்). Each denies the eye its name unless it does more than see, perceiving another's mind in 705 and looking kindly in 574.

705 says eyes that cannot read another's meaning are of no use. 393 says only the learned have eyes, and the unlearned have two sores in the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர் கல்லாதவர்). In both the physical eye is treated as worthless without a trained capacity behind it, learning in one and the reading of signs in the other.

706 says that as crystal shows what is next to it, the face shows what is strong in the heart (நெஞ்சம் கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்). 824 warns against deceivers who smile sweetly with the face while bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை). They conflict if 706 is read as holding of every face; Parimelazhagar's gloss, that the face shows what is in excess (மிக்கது) in the heart, leaves room for feeling that is kept under control.

706 says the face shows what fills the heart, as crystal shows what is beside it. 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground, and the spoken word shows the lineage of the one born in it (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும்). Both rest on காட்டும்: something visible discloses a hidden source, mood in the face and family in speech.

706 likens the face to crystal (பளிங்கு) that shows what is next to it. In 1273 a man says something shows through a young woman's beauty like the thread that shows in strung gems (மணியில் திகழ்தரு நூல்போல்). Both use a clear stone that lets something else be seen through it for an inner state appearing on the surface, as a rule about faces in 706 and as one lover's observation in the chapter on making signs known.

707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 830 advises that when an enemy turns friend one should befriend with the face and let go in the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). If the face always runs ahead of the mind, as 707 says, the control 830 recommends should not be possible; the two agree only if 707 describes the unguarded face.

707 says the face is ahead of the person in showing pleasure or anger (தான் முந்துறும்). In 1277 a woman says her bangles knew before she did that her lover had left (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). Both give the body a knowledge that arrives before the mind's own, a general observation in 707 and a lover's remark on her thinning arms in 1277.

708 says that if one has people who look within and understand what has happened, it is enough to stand looking them in the face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). 1100 says that once eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are of no use. Both make speech unnecessary between the right pair; Parimelazhagar adds for 708 that going on to speak would lessen both parties, a concern for dignity the love verse does not have.

709 says the eye will tell enmity and friendship, if one has people who understand the kinds of look (கண்ணின் வகைமை உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்). In 1097 a lover reasons that harsh little words without anger and looks like an enemy's (செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும்) are the signs of those who are close while seeming strangers. The love verse shows why 709 needs its condition: a hostile look can mean attachment, so the eye tells only those who know its kinds.

709 says the eye itself declares enmity and friendship to those who can read it. 828 says a weapon is hidden even in an enemy's hands folded in worship, and the tears his eyes shed are the same (ஒன்னார் அழுதகண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). On the reading that the eye cannot conceal, which Parimelazhagar states under 710, the weeping eye of 828 should not be able to deceive; 828 holds that it does.

710 says the measuring rod (அளக்குங்கோல்) of those who call themselves subtle is nothing but the eye. 796 says ruin has one benefit: it is a rod that measures one's people to full length (கிளைஞரை நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்). The book uses the measuring rod twice for gauging other people, the eye taking a present reading of a mind in 710 and adversity testing loyalty over time in 796.
